Lighting Committee Chair: Tim Kang Vice-Chair: Jon Miller Since its formation in 2019, the ASC MITC Lighting Committee—a group including cinematographers, lighting fixture and controller manufacturers, lighting technicians, and color scientists—has focused its efforts upon determining the best industry practices in light fixture technical standards, advanced lighting techniques, and devising educational efforts for cinematographers and lighting technicians to learn about these aforementioned developments as follows: using lithography techniques which has the promise of lower cost and lower environmental impact (Fig. 10). With these developments, Quantum Dot LED (QLED) is moving from a dual layer system to more efficient stacking structures (Fig. 11). Not to be out done, there are still many people working on LCD. One new technology is replacing the RGB filter layout, with which we are all familiar, and using a field sequential backlight system synchronized with the LCD, which would refresh at three times the framerate. The advantage being that there are no subpixels (all pixels are sequentially displaying each color) and resolution can be easily increased. Display metrology is also changing. It is not that uncommon to graph a display’s gamut in a two-dimensional CIE 1931 plot. Prior to HDR this was acceptable. But with the advent of HDR comes the realization that color is a threedimensional property, and any real measurement needs to include luminance if accurate comparison is needed. The CIE published CIE 168:2005, which defined a criteria for a three dimensional color gamut measurement. New this year, the International Committee for Display Metrology published a revised metrology standard which embraces this CIE procedure.iii But they’ve added a new twist called “Gamut Rings” based on research at NHK.4 This provides a graphic that easily shows any hue or chroma shifts as well as gamut size throughout the display’s full luminance range using CIE L*a*b* scaling as a two-dimensional graph (Fig. 12). Also added to the International Display Metrology Standard are sections on gamut intersection measurement, gamut volume, HDR measurement, color-based image retention measurement and measurement of light field displays. iiiAvailable for free at https://www.sid.org/Standards/ICDM#8271483-idms-download

MPEG-DASH Standardization For the cooperation to be effective between devices from several vendors, the required parameters and the algorithms have to be shared by all the involved HAS clients of the local network. MPEG has released a standard, DASH - part 11 to define how to deliver adaptive streaming content. The SAND (Server and Network Assisted DASH) core experiment was launched to standardize means of improving delivery through assistance of the client. Within this context, the cooperation of DASH clients has been introduced and the definition of the required parameters has been drawn. In addition, several strategies of cooperation algorithms have been specified. Rep., 2023. About the authors Erik Reinhard is a distinguished scientist at InterDigital Cesson-Sévigné, France, since June 2019. Before that, he held the same position at Technicolor R&I Cesson-Sevigné, starting in July 2013 and before that he held various academic positions at universities and research institutes in Europe and North America. He was the founder and editor-in-chief of ACM Transactions on Applied Perception and authored books on high dynamic range (HDR) imaging, color imaging, computer graphics, and natural image statistics. He has published more than 100 papers and was a member of more than 50 program committees. He was a program co-chair of six conferences and workshops, including the Eurographics Symposium on Rendering 2011. He delivered keynotes at Eurographics 2010, the Computational Color Imaging Workshop 2011, the IS&T European Conference on Color in Graphics, Imaging, and Vision 2012, the IS&T Color Imaging Conference 2022, and the ACM/SIGGRAPH Conference on Visual Media Processing 2022. He is the co-chair of the Rapporteur Group on Energy Aware Broadcasting at ITU-R and co-lead of the Study Mission on Energy Aware Service Delivery and Consumption at DVB. Finally, he won a test of time award for his color transfer paper in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications. A contribution received April 2023. Copyright © 2023 by SMPTE.

There will be a transition period during which both HDR content and SDR content are encountered in production and delivered to the end user. As such, tone mapping, either for expansion or compression, is a key feature to deliver both HDR and SDR content. Optimal results require the tone-mapping solutions that are: ■■ dynamic, to be adaptive to each individual image; ■■ tunable, so that video engineers and colorists retain control of the esthetic choices to be made in conversion; and ■■ provide an unnoticeable SDR–HDR–SDR roundtrip, to guarantee the artistic intent of the SDR source content. 28. See Farnsworth P. T. , U.S. Patent No. 2,087,683: filed April 26, 1933, issued July 20, 1937. While this patent is titled an “Image Dissector,” it was not a cold cathode tube in which the entire image passed in front of a scanning aperture to create the picture signal. It described a very advanced storage-type camera tube that used a low-velocity scanning beam from a hot cathode. It used the beam to explore a target made up of a large number of insulated areas, or “islands,” of photoelectric active material. It was planned to have the beam touch the target lightly and restore the electrons lost due to photoelectric emission. The modulated beam was to return to an anode, where its output became the picture signal. While there is no proof that Philo Farnsworth ever did build a tube of this type, its features were later incorporated by Harley Iams and Albert Rose into the RCA Orthicon and Image Orthicon camera tubes that made postwar television possible. Farnsworth's patent was so powerful that it dominated the field. This was one of Farnsworth's greatest triumphs.

See Max Dieckmann and Rudolf Hell, German (DRP) No. 450,187. Filed Apr. 5, 1925: issued Oct. 3, 1927. 8. This is from my Alexanderson/GE File. It is included in a letter from A. G. Davis to J. A. Cranston dated May 31, 1928. Also see Stephen F. Hofer, “Philo Farnsworth: The Quiet Contributor to Television,” unpublished doctoral thesis; Bowling Green University, p. 62, June 1977. At this time magnetic focus, which was the oldest existing form of focusing an electron beam, was cumbersome and suffered from severe problems due to the action of magnetic (and electrostatic) fields on the beam. When modulated, the strength of the beam altered both its velocity and its focus. Its beam charged up the screen and after a while turned itself off. In order to get sufficient brightness, it was used mainly in very-high-voltage devices and found only in specialized laboratories. It is of interest to note that Farnsworth did not include a cathode-ray receiving tube in his first application because he felt that he could not get a patent on such a basic device. Farnsworth solved the focus problem by means of a long magnetic coil (similar to the one he used on his image dissector) that reduced the deflection sensitivity, making bright pictures very difficult to achieve.

Two kinds of prefiltering are encountered in television image sensing; both progressive scan and interlaced scan sensors require optical prefiltering in both horizontal and vertical directions to prevent aliasing between high-frequency optical image information and the sensor or scanner pixel/line structure; where it is known that the reproduction of the image will use a display operating in an interlaced mode, this is a further resampling in the vertical axis; the additional vertical filtering that is required could be applied after the sensor (but before the display), but it has been common practice to apply this secondary filtering at the same time as the primary anti-aliasing filtering in the sensor. This technique cannot be used for segmented-frame image sensing—the secondary filtering must be associated only with interlaced displays in the instances these are used, otherwise vertical resolution is lost unnecessarily when the same image is displayed with progressive scanning.

3 The reference to 80, 100, or any percentage modulation of the light modulator has little significance. Reference to per cent modulation of variable-density film has no significance at all. If a modulator such as a light valve, deflected penumbra, or glow lamp, has fixed average intensity, the modulation may be then stated definitely in terms of percentages of complete or 100 per cent modulation. In this case, 100 per cent modulation is that level at which the amplitude of the wave is equal to the average or mean value of light intensity in which case the excursion of light intensity extends from zero to double the mean.

The use of bias (for ground noise reduction) and reverse bias (for level range extension) has complicated this concept. However, for a reference point, some arbitrarily chosen mean value of light intensity is established, and the percentage modulation is referred to this. The use of this mean value and 100 per cent modulation thereof imposes upon the film an excursion of exposure which the film may accommodate with reasonably low distortion. This is the customary procedure in studio recording practice. The percentage modulation values referred to herein are so reckoned.

5 The over-all effective gamma determined in this manner is the gamma of a simple curve, T p = KE n γ having only a single value of gamma, which curve includes the 2 points used for the computation of gamma. Generally, film characteristics as used in practice involve not only the straight portion of the H and D curve, but the toe and shoulder as well. The positive film H and D toe region is extensively used in variable-density sound recording. The curve involving both the straight line and toe portions requires multiple values of gamma for expression. To express such a curve in terms of gamma, and to take delta-db data to compute gamma, requires that the curve be scanned in short increments. The gamma for each increment as defined by 2 exposure values should be calculated by use of Formula 2. In practice it has been learned that the over-all effective gamma should not exceed unity to any appreciable extent in any portion of the film characteristic curve. Gamma in excess of unity is equivalent to expansion, and is particularly deterimental to speech intelligibility. Compression in the same degree is acceptable. Thus, if low and medium level recordings, made with ground noise reduction, are confined to the straight portion of the H and D curve (which portion has an over-all effective gamma of unity or only slightly higher), the higher level recordings will extend into the region of the toe of the positive H and D curve where the gamma is lower and some compression is encountered. This is the preferred condition of variable-density recording technique. For routine checking, 3 delta-db control points are required; the first at bias value of exposure, the second at unbias, and the third at reverse bias. The gamma as computed from the first two should lie between unity and 5 per cent greater. The gamma as computed from the second and third should lie between unity and 10 per cent less than unity. The ability to check these 2 ranges separately is a unique advantage enjoyed by the delta-db test over the intermodulation test. For this paper, the term “Effective Over-all Gamma” has been adopted to represent the exponent of the over-all response curve, which is plotted with the current in the modulator as the abscissa and the photocell output current as ordinates. Effective over-all gamma thus includes all factors in the system which affect contrast or linearity, and is the figure which must be reduced to unity for linear performance of the system. The use of the term gamma in this manner has aroused some criticism, but the criticism is based upon academic rather than practical considerations.

10. “Average modulation level” is interpreted here as the average white level minus the average black level (for color channels read light for white and dark for black). The average white level is maximum white response (the maximum level across the white tilted bar) plus minimum white response (the minimum level across the white tilted bar) divided by two. Similarly, average black level is maximum black response (that is the maximum level across the black tilted bar) plus minimum black response (the minimum level across the black tilted bar) divided by two. In all these measurements, the effect of random noise must be removed. In our measurements, we use frame-to-frame averaging and spatial averaging across the test pattern and alias patterns. Note that average modulation level is also used in measuring the contrast transfer function (CTF) of a system. Thus, aliasing amplitude is the product of alias ratio, CTF, and image contrast.

Negative film has significant “exposure latitude”; which is generally exploited more than the latitude available in video cameras; hence during or after telecine transfer it may be necessary to expand part of the recovered density range of an over- or under-exposed negative to yield a satisfactory grayscale. This means more amplitude coding levels are required to avoid visible quantizing errors. Where this grayscale correction is deferred (e.g., in so-called “tape-to-tape” color correction), all equipment prior to this correction must maintain this greater precision (larger dynamic range).

15. “Segmented” form means that the active lines from the total progressive frame, in this case 1080, are divided into odd-numbered lines (540) in a first segment, and the remaining even-numbered lines (540) in a second segment. The segment occurrence rate is then twice the progressive frame rate. There are two differences between this form and the more familiar interlaced form. First, this mode is confined to applications where the original source prior to segmentation has been scanned with a progressive scan sensor (e.g., film); this means that the motion phase of the two segments will be the same (which is not the case with true interlaced scanning). Second, it is required that there be no additional built-in vertical response filtering (e.g., by line-averaging in the sensor), as is the case with interlaced scanning, and which is present to prevent small area flicker and aliasing in interlaced displays. This is because “segmented” signals are intended to be converted back to progressive scan at some later stage. The purpose of this segmentation is to allow easier adaptation of equipment designed originally for interlaced operation, such as VTRs, and also via the doubling of effective vertical rate (in this case from 24 Hz to 48 Hz) to allow simple monitoring with a tolerable flicker frequency.

Using Compressed Domain Tile Stitching, all the stitched tiles change spatial position within the RoI during such an event. Therefore, random access usually would have to be provided for all the tiles leading to a significant peak bitrate increase compared to classic Tiled Panorama Streaming without stitching. In order to resolve this disadvantage, Fraunhofer HHI has developed a lightweight processing that operates in the compressed domain.5 Through inserting artificial reference pictures into the bitstream at RoI change events with low complexity and for almost zero bitrate cost, tiles that remain in the RoI, e.g., Tiles 3 and 4 in Fig. 10, can use temporal prediction as in the classic Tiled Panorama Streaming approach. Hence, among other advantages, the peak bitrate behavior using Compressed Domain Tile Stitching with a single decoder instance on the end device is comparable to classic Tiled Panorama Streaming that requires multiple decoders. Conclusion We have presented in this paper a set of video distortion metrics that could prove to be particularly useful for HDR video. The main motivating principle we presented was the “spatial detail” signal, which we used in two ways: (1) as a proxy for the original image data and (2) as a guide to the perceptually important features in HDR WCG video. The spatial detail signal is a condensed version of the original image that preserves the recognizable details in an image while discounting local luminance. From a practical standpoint, the important key characteristic of the spatial detail signal is that it is statistically stable having an expectably compact, peaked, biphasic, and symmetric distribution of values that is preserved across a wide range in images and video. Larger values—positive and negative—form a convenient guide to the kinds of features people tend to find significant. The spatial detail values nearer the zero midpoint of the distribution form a convenient guide to image regions that people would tend to classify as background or textural. Such feature and texture maps provide a stable framework in which to selectively investigate the perceptual potent highlights and dark details that are the hallmark of HDR video. Using the spatial detail as a proxy for the original image, we showed that correlation between the spatial detail signals of the uncompressed and compressed versions of HDR video was systematically affected by the aggressiveness of HEVC compression. By combining spatial detail correlation with our feature and texture assignment methods, we showed that texture correlation was impacted significantly more than feature correlation. Spatial detail correlation has several distinctions compared to established video quality metrics. It can be used selectively on bright and dark features and on textures. Moreover, spatial detail values are in the range of 0 to 1, which is more intuitive than the unbounded PSNR scale, while being a much more sensitive indicator than MS-SSIM over the range of compression levels typical of TV services. We have deliberately used the term “video distortion” instead of “video quality” throughout this paper. The main reason for doing so is that the metrics we proposed have not yet been compared to subjective test scores and thus may not yet be claimed to be a calibrated predictor of subjective video quality scores. For this reason, we utilized a single CPU system. Display We support a variety of target displays in our stitching pipeline. These include a regular 4K computer display, an HMD, and a Pufferfish display. Computer Display In the case of a standard 16:9 4K computer display, the panorama resulting from the video stitching operation is texture mapped onto the inside of a sphere. The viewer is placed into the center of the sphere with a 180° field of view projected onto the flat computer display. This method was used to validate our implementation and to permit different people to view our realtime results. HMD The stitched panorama was also rendered for an Oculus VR headset using the OpenVR38 toolkit. This rendered view allows the wearer of the HMD to see the whole 360 view from the position of the camera by looking around. Because the content is video and the camera is stationary, the viewer cannot zoom, but only pan and tilt to see the complete 360° view. Spherical Display In an effort to provide a spherical projection that could be viewed by more than one person, useful for on-set review and monitoring of captured content, we support and also use a Pufferfish spherical display39 by Pufferfish, Ltd. of Edinburgh for our realtime streaming demonstration at SIGGRAPH 2016 as shown in Fig. 3. K. He et al., “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition,” Proc. IEEE Conf. Comput. Vision Patt. Recogn., pp. 770–778, 2016. Conclusion The rapid rise of AI is disrupting many industries. Using AI for automating tasks previously done by human operators allows cost-efficient deployment and development of many large-scale applications that were unfeasible before. In this paper, we presented how AI can contribute to fighting piracy. We analyzed which aspects of AI are applicable in the implementation of large-scale content monitoring systems that track and identify illegally distributed content. We demonstrated how AI can be trained for automatically recognizing the original source of a video stream, by analyzing the logo of the content distributor from whom the content has been pirated. We see this as a building block into more complex content monitoring systems, which integrate multiple AI components for real-time monitoring of redistribution of copyrighted material.

Welch, “Simplifying Video Delivery Management,” presented at the SCTE Cable-Tec Expo 2011, Atlanta, GA, Nov. 2011. ■■ During a major sports package launch, it was determined through passive intra-CDN monitoring that all end-user traffic was being supplied from a single cache node due to a DNS issue. Rather than the intended conf ig uration of distr ibuting client requests to different cache nodes, all requests were routed to a single cache which, in turn, resulted in the origin server requests originating from only one cache. This resulted in poor performance for many end clients due to cache server oversubscription. ■■ During a sports package launch event, postedge cache passive monitoring showed that a game console client was only buffering one segment at a time. This led to frequent buffer underflows causing frequent rebuffering events and playback stalls impacting the playback experience quality. ■■ Intra-CDN passive monitoring led to the discovery that a server misconfiguration was erroneously set to time out and delete content causing caching to repeatedly fail and resulting in excessive origin server requests. Service rapidly became unusable. ■■ A CDN vendor reported to a customer that issues were caused by excessively long response time from the customer’s origin server. Intra-CDN monitoring proved this was not the case and pointed instead to CDN issues. ■■ A CDN vendor was not accurately logging HTTP response failures. Independent active synthetic client testing identified the HTTP response codes enabling rapid troubleshooting of the issue. ■■ Active synthetic client testing highlighted a “stalled” manifest condition causing content to loop on client players. ■■ Post-CDN synthetic client monitoring raised a high volume of VeriStream alarms indicating end-user clients may be having buffering issues. The early warning allowed for on-the-fly CDN tuning to proactively eliminate the delays and prevent end-user experience degradation. ■■ Intra-CDN passive monitoring identified a load balancer with performance issues under load. Early warning allowed the problem to be fixed before customers were impacted. All of these issues were rapidly identified by having sufficient realtime measurement data available and in a form that enabled system managers to pinpoint issues. Many incidents enabled managers to take action quickly before incidents escalated. In other cases, the measurement data enabled targeted corrective action after the event by providing data that likely would not have been available without realtime monitoring. Conclusion We carried out subjective tests with 60 viewers over the age of 18, which were termed adult viewers, and with 570 young students under the age of 17, the majority being 10 or 11 years old, which were termed student viewers. We believe that the use of such a large population of viewers, with such a range of ages, makes this a very rare, if not unique, experiment. The aim of the experiment was to understand the relative annoyance caused by various transmission impairments when viewing television content, and to study the impact of the type of screen on which the content is viewed, considering viewing on tablets and on a TV, and to study the impact of the age of the viewer. We found a significant level of consistency from the overall results of our experiments. We found the following results: that interruptions are the most annoying impairment that was tested, multiple short interruptions are more annoying than a single longer interruption of the same duration, and it is more annoying when the interruption causes some of the content not to be presented, rather than just a pause. It was observed that dropping to a very low quality for a short period of time and dropping to a medium quality for a longer period are more annoying while watching on a TV than on a tablet. Compared to the adult viewers, younger viewers are more sensitive to impairments when viewing on a tablet while older viewers are more sensitive to impairments when viewing on a TV. A reasonably high level of similarity exists between the opinions of the adult viewers and the student viewers, suggesting to some extent that the relative annoyance caused by different impairments is independent of age. The experiment and its results also show that students, as young as 10 or 11 years of age, can be used as viewers in video subjective testing if the test is designed appropriately, which in this experiment meant using short test sessions of 6 min each. We hope that the results obtained will influence the design of future television content delivery services, so that if transmission impairments do occur, the service is designed to minimize the annoyance caused. We also hope that we motivate other researchers to include young students in their experiments, not only because their views are valid, but also to give them direct experience of work in the technology industry and hence to encourage them to study STEM9 subjects to achieve a rewarding career in the industry.

A test series was conducted with 2 (SD), 6 (HD), and 10 (HD) Mb/s H.264 HD proxy. Again, a reference HP Z4 workstation and an office client served as the basis. A red x indicates cases in which the quality of the proxy was not sufficient. A light green arrow signifies cases that can be performed with proxy editing, but would require a final approval, ideally on the used HiRes or rendered clip. The dark green fields have been approved as cases which can be realized with proxy editing only. It is obvious that several cases cannot be done with 2 Mb/s SD proxy, since the resolution does not allow the evaluation of sharpness, focal length or other technical parameters. Based on the parameters, a proxy will not match the quality of the original HiRes file, but utilizing an H.264 video codec with full HD resolution and a bit rate between 6 and 10 Mb/s, results can be achieved that are acceptable to editors without significant detriment to the user experience. HD proxy shows good results on “standard” edits such as titling, rough editing, simple effects, graphical templates, and multicamera productions, whereas elaborate editing, which requires technical evaluation and sophisticated graphics, pushes the limits of proxy editing. For those cases, a viable setup could be a combination of HD proxy editing, with proxy hosted in the cloud and HiRes editing on premise. Several edits can already be done and finished remotely, but when required, those edits can be completed on premise or exchanged with editors, which have access to the HiRes files. Conclusion This article has reviewed different network architectures that provide a better QoE for ABR delivery. Encoding, especially CAE, is key to providing the best QoE. CMAF is an essential technology to reduce the ABR delivery end-to-end latency to a level close to what broadcast offers. CDN caching is an important factor, and client acceleration should also be considered. Finally, to optimize the network resources and avoid unfair client behavior, we advise operators to deploy a network optimization technology. All of those elements make us confident that, in the very near future, an ABR delivery mechanism can be close to a broadcast delivery network on a managed network. On an unmanaged network, it would be more of a challenge, as several parameters are out of the control of the OTT service provider.

Conclusion We have upgraded our 8K 240-frames/sec camera system by adding three new modes: 480-frames/sec shooting, 120-frames/sec random noise reduction shooting, and 120-frames/sec flicker reduction shooting. In the 480-frames/sec shooting mode, we captured 8K 480-frames/sec images without visible lag by operating the image sensor at double the normal speed. However, the SNR of 480-frames/sec images was degraded more than expected. Therefore, it is necessary to improve image sensor operation in the 480-frames/sec mode to obtain a reasonable image quality. We also confirmed the effectiveness of random noise reduction and flicker reduction in the 120-frames/ sec shooting mode. These image quality improvement functions can be applied to various video cameras and will be introduced in future 8K cameras as required functions. We will continue to improve the image quality of the 480-frames/sec images and utilize the camera system for various 8K content productions by using the newly added functions. Reception Method Using a Receiving System With POF Cable POFs5,6 are used in data centers and elsewhere. We have developed equipment for receiving satellite broadcasting using POFs. Quartz glass singlemode fibers (SMFs) are often used as optical fibers in many broadcasting/communication installations, such as fiber to the home (FTTH). Although the signal attenuation and other characteristics of POFs are inferior to those of glass-based SMFs, their high flexibility and tolerance to shaft misalignment mean that POFs are unaffected by problems common to quartz glass SMFs, such as workability, safety, and bend resistance. In Japan, 64% of apartment blocks consist of smalland medium-sized buildings of five stories or less. In this case, since the transmission distance from the antenna to the television is about 100 m or less, signal attenuation is within an allowable range when using a POF receiving system. Moreover, since POFs are thin and have excellent flexibility compared with conventional coaxial cables, flexible installation is possible. A system using a POF connection is shown in Fig. 12. Video Services Forum (VSF) Technical Recommendation TR-06-1, “Reliable Internet Stream Transport (RIST) Protocol Future Work Future studies that did not fit into the scope of this paper are: ■■ Jitter characteristics: Study the jitter characteristics that the different implementations add. Ideally, the pattern of interpacket gaps on the input of the sender should be recreated exactly on the output of the receiver. ■■ End-to-end latency: Another interesting area to study is the full end-to-end latency; this study has considered the situation where each protocol has an identically sized latency buffer. ■■ Congestion control: This study has not attempted to push the protocols to the limit with regard to congestion control, which is something that should be explored further. ■■ Quality of experience: As suggested earlier, studying the quality of experience instead of pure packet drop statistics is also very important. A different way to present the data in a study such as this one, albeit a more workintensive method, could be to decide on an acceptable rate of residual packet drops and to attempt to determine the boundaries in line drop rate that allows the protocols to stay within that acceptable residual drop rate. That is, what are the worst conditions that each protocol can be subjected to and still perform acceptably. Additionally, the measurements could be presented in the form of errored seconds instead, that is, a count of the number of seconds that contain any dropped packets. It may be that for two implementations with the same residual drop rate, one of them has the loss more grouped and thus has fewer errored seconds, which may lead to fewer visible artifacts. ■■ High-bandwidth ARQ transport: With cloud being leveraged also for high-end workflows, performing similar benchmarks with much greater bandwidths, such as a 3 Gb/s JPEG-XS compressed ultrahigh-definition (UHD) signal, would be of interest. In addition, as bandwidths grow well into the multiple of 10 Gb/s range, there are also performance aspects when it comes to the platform itself. For example, from a CPU/memory perspective, is there a tradeoff between ARQ and FEC for pure execution purposes at these high speeds? Conclusion In the last year alone, retransmission technology has gained a lot of attention, driven by both initiatives such as the SRT Alliance and RIST, but also as a consequence of the industry starting to realize the importance of the technology as cloud starts to cement itself further as a key part of the broadcast workflow. The two major open alternatives in the market, RIST and SRT, all have backing from a large number of vendors and broadcasters. But this is in a market that is already a decade in the making in terms of proprietary solutions and ecosystems. Therefore, while RIST and SRT are technically good alternatives already today, the large proprietary ecosystems already in place are likely to exist for many years, while being augmented by these new challengers.

Another limitation was the logical mapping between the quality factor representative values and the probability distribution. The fundamental assumption of the SDT framework is normal probability distributions for the signal and errors.38 Therefore, a mapping function that better reflects the real distribution of each quality factor should lead to more accurate user models. A third important limitation was the small participant sample. Adding more participants would increase the opportunity of collecting representative data, and the larger sample size would increase the power of statistical analysis and the developed prediction models. Future research could include a fine-tuning stage where active learning algorithms are employed.56,57 Active learning will allow the system to learn directly from humans by querying the caption quality. The selection algorithm would prioritize caption variations that had greater uncertainty associated with them, providing a more efficient training process. Conclusion In this paper, the design and development of a novel system to assess the quality of CC based on caption viewer subjective quality ratings is described. Based on findings from a user study with hearing-impaired viewers, a set of human decision probability models dealing with captioning variations was developed. With these user models and prediction models, we then generated artificial data, which reflected human assessment of caption quality. We then trained deep neural networks with the generated data, creating an AI system to predict human subjective ratings for different caption variations. The proposed solution fills a gap in existing quality assessment models for CC, which does not include any viewer quality assessment factors. The proposed system should improve as more data are collected, allowing the core prediction model to learn from the new user data over time.

Conclusion In this study, we investigated the suitability of objective quality metrics for compressed HDR/WCG images encoded with HLG. Our main findings are three. First, the chroma components must be taken into account by objective metrics, because HDR metrics that consider only the luminance channel fail to detect color distortions that observers can notice; second, the results of the investigated metrics that do consider color are nonetheless worse than the results of VIF, despite the fact that VIF is applied only on the luminance; and third, each color difference metric behaves differently depending on the type of the test image. Based on these results, as future work, we will study the aggregation of metrics into a single one as a solution to the open problem of finding an objective metric for HLG-encoded HDR/WCG content.

Conclusion This study compares the performance of emerging MPEG-5 EVC and H.266/MPEG-VVC video compression standards with that of their predecessor H.265/MPEG-HEVC. In addition, given the growing popularity of the AV1 video codec, AV1 is included as an alternative baseline. Particularly, it was determined that the coding gain of VVC in terms of BD-BR PSNRYUV is larger than that of EVC, and it is about 40% for encoding 4K/2160p video sequences; however, this comes with a very significant computational complexity increase by a factor of more than 9 compared to HEVC and by a factor of approximately 2 compared to EVC. In turn, EVC achieves bitrate savings of about 30% for 4K/2160p encoding. On the other hand, for encoding FHD/1080p video sequences, VVC achieves bitrate savings of ~37% over HEVC, while the corresponding bitrate savings of EVC are ~23%. Furthermore, when testing the AV1 encoder in a twopass VBR mode, for the 4K/2160p and FHD/1080p encoding, it was found that AV1 provides bitrate savings of ~20% and ~24%, respectively. Based on the extensive experimental results presented in this work for a wide range of resolutions, frame rates, and bit depths, the authors find both EVC and VVC to be very promising successors to HEVC. However, the jury is still out on the speed of their adoption.

As found in Experiment 1, a red foreground object stands out well, catches viewers’ attention, and should be rated as a highlighted region-of-interest object for computational purposes. The data shows significant viewer preference for Display A when PCLCOLOR exceeded 20%. The viewers overwhelmingly chose the display with more saturated colors and narrower primary color bandwidth. In one case, image # 53, viewers split their decision. This particular picture contained the brightest white (around a light fixture), but significantly less saturated color than any other pictures in the set. In terms of choosing a brighter or more vivid picture, our hypothesis is confirmed in a qualitative fashion and should be followed by another experiment to assess viewer reaction in degrees of PCLCOLOR. We note another singular result for image # 69 where viewers predominately favored Display A. However, the PCL ratio is the highest score in this test set, yet not preferred unanimously as might be expected by such a high computational score. This image will also be a subject of further study in a future phase. Excluding this one outlier, the subjective scoring correlated well with the PCL ratio, as shown by a Pearson correlation equal to 0.93. Discussion The evidence, both computationally and subjectively, supports integrating Nayatani’s model for H–K effect amplification with iCAM06 HDR image analysis. Furthermore, we used a critical reference display, but while valid, such a display is not practical for multiple demonstrations. Some HDR displays and certain cinema projectors in the market are expanding the boundaries of color range beyond DCI-P3; therefore, our study of colors beyond DCI-P3 is relevant. This paper has described a metrology and display analysis procedure that quantifies the brightness amplification when displays render highly saturated colors that extend beyond DCI-P3. However, we stopped short of recommending how the content delivery ecosystem should adapt to the study. There is prolific evidence of material technologies, such as quantum dot, increasing the primary color saturation and expanding the colors viewable on a display. We call for an industry dialogue to consider how to implement a production flow that makes use of greater and brighter color. SMPTE published SMPTE 428-121 and SMPTE 431-1 in 2006; it is natural to expect that state-of-the-art displays today can produce more colors that consumers will find desirable. Conclusion In this paper, we studied the differences between onpremise broadcast and cloud-based online video delivery workflows and identified the means needed to bridge the gaps between them. These include improvements in cloud ingest, signal processing stacks, transcoder capabilities, and most importantly, a broadcast-grade cloud playout system. Although current deployments require multicast gateways as external hardware devices, it is perfectly reasonable to assume that they could be digitized and located inside the customers’ User Agent devices. BBC R&D group’s attempt to digitalize multicast gateway through WebAssembly was halted due to poor browser support for server push cache manipulation.2 Once the browsers and smartphones start introducing support for more loose Push cache manipulation, it might reignite the interest in bringing that idea to life. In a perfect world, the browsers should be capable of multicast QUIC stream reception completely software-based, without any intermediary devices. QUIC can be coupled with advanced forward errorcorrection schemes like fountain or network codes,31 which will effectively enable proactive error correction over the multicast link, further reducing the signaling overhead and even potentially removing the need for the return link and long buffering times due to retransmission, keeping delivery latencies as low as possible. Related to the ATSC 3.0 test-bed in Copenhagen, the result of this project was to better understand the possibilities and benefits of using QUIC instead of UDP as the network transport protocol, independent of the application layer protocols used ecosystem. In an ATSC 3.0 setup, multicast is used in a variety of ways with most transport protocols relying on UDP with error correction, as TCP will only impose the previously described problems. With the use of QUIC, reliability is taken to a new level, and the intention is to use QUIC in the entire chain from ingestion to presentation on the end-user device. The project only followed the distribution of media content using HTTP/3 over QUIC in an infrastructure always relying on two-way communication available in all distribution entities, for example, the CDN scenario. The next step is to integrate QUIC into the IP broadcast ecosystem, using a modified ROUTE protocol over ATSC 3.0 and DVB-GSE as bearer technologies and reaching the gateway. The reliability of QUIC, in the presented implementation, will depend on the broadband available at the gateway. Alternative methods exist, using forward error correction in separate ROUTE repair sessions [13], to carry out stream repair at the gateway without the need for an active internet connection. This is to ensure a reliable reception even at locations with a very poor or no internet connectivity. Preliminary trails have been carried out, and the results will be presented in a separate article. Conclusion The efforts of the Dailies QC Working Group are a first step toward implementing a consistent, sustainable dailies QC workflow that is collaboratively defined by a broad group of industry professionals. Universal adoption of this terminology, taxonomy, best practice, and general framework means that more software can be developed to automate basic tracking and QC work. Additionally, the people who need to know about things going wrong get the right information more efficiently, and productions can easily outsource work to freelancers and global networks who all understand the core structure and responsibilities of the tasks. The Dailies QC Working Group is the beginning of a conversation about how we can build a solid foundation for the future of dailies as an aspect of filmmaking. Globally, dailies are becoming a crucial part of the future of the screen industry, with timeand cost-saving opportunities to be realized across the sector. As both big studios and independent companies develop their own version of a more automated workf low, we aim to open up the lines of communication, break down the silos of innovation, and allow more people to harness the collaborative efforts of the dailies teams and their work to benefit future productions. With these automation and standardization efforts happening within different studios, now is a great time to start communicating between these groups to develop more consistent workf lows. There is still a great amount of collaborative work to be done to realize a standard within dailies processes. We believe that this is the first step outside of any particular company that aims to future-proof key components of the dailies workf low, save money and time, and allow us all to work smarter rather than harder. The taxonomy described in this paper is a living document and a reference resource that productions, technologists, and studios can use when developing their own workflows and tools. Blacks in STEM Jobs Are Especially Concerned About Diversity and Discrimination Conclusion There is no question about the direction the industry is heading when it comes to incorporating AI and machine learning. As this technology improves, newer algorithms are being written and neural networks are being created to “think” more like a human brain. However, it is still a complicated process that relies on humans training the systems to search for specific data sets and modeling of human behavior. And ultimately, M&E is oriented around audiovisual art, which will always have a high level of subjectivity. We will best integrate art with automation by embracing our humanity further. We need to recognize how our human needs, curiosities, and perspectives make workflows better. We must prioritize encouraging people from diverse backgrounds to become workflow professionals so that their unique perspectives can contribute to pushing the M&E industry to be more efficient for all types of people and content. As we continue to learn about and shape these workflows, we need to engage more with experts in AI ethics and data science to further understand possibilities and pitfalls. Until technology can fully replicate human behavior and psychology, humans will always be a necessary part of a workflow. Making sure we address the shortfalls of technology while establishing the best environment for humans to succeed is important. We must also remember the workflow of the past to not fall into the same ethical traps as our predecessors. By having a diverse talent pool, working to combat the biases inherent in AI, and using automation intentionally and thoughtfully, we can create inclusive and efficient workflows to support an industry of authentic storytelling.

Application 2: Facial Expression Summaries We now turn our attention to another application that the proposed system naturally lends itself to, namely the automatic generation of facial expression summaries. In this setting, rather than looking for similar facial expressions, the aim here is to find dissimilar ones. Figure 8 shows an example facial expression summary where we extracted faces for Jim Carrey from a range of movies and shows he starred in. To group similar facial expressions, we use agglomerative clustering (with N = 10 clusters, using ward linkage and Euclidean distance) on facial embeddings extracted from all faces recognized as Jim Carrey. In the figure, we show one representative face for each of the ten clusters. As can be seen, most of the facial expressions shown here are very different from the ones exhibited in the six basic emotions and hence systems trained on basic emotions would not be able to distinguish them in such detail. Furthermore, the above example also reinforces the importance of being able to search facial expressions via a “reference” face, as it would be very hard to give a name/tag to most of these faces. Conclusion We have presented a system that can classify custom facial expressions in videos. Additionally, we observe that for some transformed coefficient distributions, and given the context adaptive binary arithmetic coding (CABAC) context, a small QP decrease may result in almost no rate increment. This can be explained by two facts. First, the CABAC context may be better suited when changing QP, making the entropy coding of quantized coefficients more efficient. Second, a slight quantized coefficient bitrate increase can be compensated by the differential QP syntax bitrate decrease. These two cases generate a lower rate than foreseen that we name “rate-drop.” Overall, refining locally a set of QP candidates can, at the same time, be beneficial for both rate and distortion, without compromising any global RDO, and that is what LQR does. Finally, thanks to additional heuristics and optimizations (e.g., distortion estimation in the transform domain), the LQR implementation can be kept reasonable in terms of computation overhead, with an overall encoding runtime increase measured below 10% in a MediaKind optimized software HEVC encoder. The compression efficiency performance of the LQR algorithm combined with STAQ (RDSTQ), implemented into ×265 and using JCT-VC common test conditions, is summarized in Table 3. Complementary to the STAQ algorithm, the coding efficiency advantage is about 6% bitrate saving for the same PSNR- or SSIMbased quality. Conclusion By sharing an overview of the hybrid video coding scheme that holds for most modern video compression standards, we highlight the key role of the quantization in optimizing the video quality/bitrate tradeoff, as the (almost) only adjustable lossy processing step in any encoding system. We consequently detail the various levels of granularity and control points available for quantization optimization, most notably the block or CU-level QP adaptation. As practical examples, we introduce and share some insights on two differentiating quantization algorithms, namely STAQ and LQR. Some APIs such as the Networked Media Open Specifications (NMOS) APIs for registration, discovery, and connection management have been successful. Other efforts, perhaps less so. And while the idea of a common set of APIs for media seems interesting, a number of factors may keep this out of reach. It is likely that bespoke APIs will always be a part of media infrastructures. Given this, are there best practices from the IT world we can adopt with regard to media APIs. The definitive answer is “yes.” A survey by programmableweb.com22 found that “developers want clearly documented APIs that are reliably available.” In fact, the desire for “Complete and accurate documentation” was rated even higher than service availability or service responsiveness! Well-documented code is clearly a priority. The IT industry has been stressing the benefits of well-written, self-describing APIs for years. And in fact, there has been a robust discussion of what makes a good API versus a bad one for many years as well.23 As we move to a more IT-centric media world, it would behoove us to learn from the IT world’s mistakes with regard to the documentation of APIs. Well-written self-describing APIs have several characteristics. They do one thing well, they are simple to understand and use, they do not require special knowledge of what is going on behind the interface to implement the API, and they contain information and documentation, and sometimes even tests, that aid developers in creating successful implementations. For a pretty exhaustive discussion of what it takes to make a good API, see “How to Design a Good API and Why it Matters,” written by Joshua Bloch, principal software engineer at Google.24 Technologies such as Swagger25 and Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) such as the Eclipse IDE26 help enforce good behaviors in API development and support “code first” environments where, once the user requirements are understood, developers immediately start writing code to address those requirements. The documentation is essentially developed alongside the code. Conclusion This article has introduced a number of key concepts that have helped the IT industry deliver the “ilities” that their users demand (flexibility, scalability, reusability, and so on). We now find ourselves in a position where media consumers are requesting those same “ilities.” A potential way forward would be to carefully consider how we can adopt the bedrock principles in this article that have enabled modern IT and computing. Available: https://www.mile-high.video/_files/ugd/3b5446_2ccbd408c67245cabf3c9bae36b39145.pdfRight Time for Migrating SR in the Headend Up to now, upscaling to 4K has been deployed in end-user devices, such as UHD 4K TVs, but not on the headend side before delivery. The main reason is that UHD 4K TVs took a significant market share in the last few years, while the vast majority of linear channels throughout the world are still in SD or HD resolutions. The number of UHD 4K channels is still limited, because of the extra bandwidth needed to deliver higher resolution. For the targeted bandwidth capacity, the delivery in HD resolution and upscaling into 4K in the TV has been judged as good enough. Based on the evaluations above, this type of upscaling cannot offer a “true” 4K experience similar to what SR could achieve. Moreover, when the HD content suffers from compression artifacts due to bandwidth constraints, these artifacts can be amplified by the upscaling process, leading to a very disappointing 4K experience. Embedding CPU-intensive deep restoration (DR)/SR algorithms in end-user devices may not be economically feasible or good for the planet’s power consumption, but embedding these algorithms in the headend before delivery only makes sense if 4K can be delivered with a sufficient quality at a reasonable bandwidth (i.e., limited extra bandwidth compared with HD). It will not be long before this happens because there are powerful technologies on the horizon that will enable it. There are, of course, new codecs, appearing on the market, such as AV1,11 as well as codecs just being standardized, such as Versatile Video Coding (VVC)12 and Essential Video Coding (EVC).13 However, it may take a few years before these codecs become mainstream. Alternative technologies can make use of already deployed codecs, such as HEVC, and be applied in a straightforward manner to 4K delivery, with compatibility for the millions of devices already deployed. Low complexity enhancement video coding (LCEVC),14 which has just been standardized by MPEG, is one option with a two-layer encoding scheme. Dynamic resolution encoding (DRE), which is already deployed by Netflix for video on demand (VOD) delivery and can be applied for live delivery thanks to artificial intelligence (AI),15 is another one. These two technologies can limit the extra bandwidth of 4K delivery compared with HD delivery at a very reasonable level and make the upscaling of 4K in the headend a good option. Conclusion This article has shown that SR techniques are now mature enough to be used in the professional video market and deliver a “true” 4K experience with digital video content captured at a lower resolution. The complexity of the algorithm under study is compatible with upscaling live HD content into 4K. For archives with a lower resolution and poor quality, it is recommended to first apply deep restoration and noise reduction processes that will preferably run offline and be trained to address specific degradation.

This paper first presented an evaluation setup for systematically evaluating the time synchronization precision between a wireless device and a wired PTP Grandmaster. The article presented results, focusing on the technical feasibility of precise time synchronization over a wireless link. The evaluation showed that a synchronization accuracy of less than 4 μs can be achieved with residence time measured and reported by the 5G system compared to ~120–150 μs without the 5G network inserting the residence time. The accuracy difference between the linear regression and PI servo with additional tweaks was negligible. Therefore, based on these results, a more hassle-free linear regression servo can be used whenever available without any performance degradation. These results prove the possibility of using such a system for conventional media production over 5G, where the genlock or sampling references are generated locally by a media device receiving the timing information from a network via PTP. For high-performance uncompressed media like the ST 2110 and the precise packet pacing required by the ST 2110-21, the reported accuracy is insufficient in the current technological iteration. However, it is unlikely that uncompressed video will be transported over a 5G network due to radio spectrum availability. In summary, the authors still believe that the results appear promising for potential use for compressed solutions. Upcoming iterations of the 5G spec introducing additional timing and media-specific functionality and improved high-efficiency low latency encoding technologies may ensure such use cases. Future experiments may look closer at the precision of the offset measurements through the 5G systems and additional practical use cases using various compression technologies.

Conclusion Semantic indexing is a new method of searching for and retrieving media files that uses ML to extract and encode semantic representations found in various media formats. This allows for searches using unstructured text queries, which can be faster and more accurate than traditional metadata searches. Semantic representations can also be used to provide insights into the media library. The CLIP model from OpenAI is one example of a model that can be used for semantic indexing, and the Elasticsearch database can be used to store the resulting embeddings. There are many potential applications for semantic search, including finding media with queries that contain summaries or synonyms, using learned cultural knowledge. Additionally, semantic search can be extended to use multiple languages for queries and used to find additional media types like video clips and audio files. Next Steps Recently, the EBU, Movie labs, and SMPTE published a primer29 on using semantic technologies, which, among the various uses, lists contextual search and discovery as one of the benefits. The approach outlined in that primer discusses using a knowledge graph of triples stored in graph databases to relate semantically linked data. This approach is an alternate, if not complementary, approach to semantic search using embeddings. Prior to the primer mentioned earlier, Wei et al.30 provided a comprehensive overview of semantic search systems based on linked data. Semantically linked systems provide for usage that can go beyond conventional search usage. The entity-relationship graph lends itself to queries that go beyond resolving a search query to a digital asset. The entity relationships can be used to discover hitherto unknown relationships between data records and digital assets by traversing edges in the graph to provide insights and recommendations;31 to organize the data in predefined structures, making traversal and automation possible; to connect heterogeneous and distributed data sources while maintaining data integrity. Most of these knowledge graph-based systems require standardized predefined ontologies and a-priori-defined taxonomies to model the relationships. In contrast, text embedding-based systems can discover the taxonomy. Next steps include comparing the architectures and results of using semantic embeddings versus this new approach to knowledge graphs for searching media libraries. Part of the investigation is to evaluate if the technologies complement each other rather than being distinct approaches.

The “default” graph shows again the performance of an “all-intra” configuration. In the “inter=intra” configuration, the quantizer configuration for inter- and intracoded coefficients is identical. In all remaining configurations, it is offset in the positive or negative direction by one or multiple bitplanes. The “intra Q reduced by 1” indicates a configuration where intracoded coefficients are quantized by one additional bitplane relative to intercoded coefficients, that is, intra is quantized coarser. As seen in the plots, this leads to consistently worse performance regardless of the nature of the image, though it impacts mostly the low-PSNR end for natural images and the high-PSNR end for screen content. Small PSNR gains can be reached if the quantization of intra-coefficients is finer than that of interpredicted coefficients, with the peak performance at a relative quantization shift of 2 bitplanes. The overall PSNR gains remain, however, relatively moderate, approximately 0.2 dB for the above test images. To validate this content-aware approach for video game content, we compared it to a reference case where encoding tools are dynamically enabled in a fixed order, independent of the input content, and defined to maximize the compression efficiency on natural content. Both configurations were run in the same computational resources and only standard encoding tools were included in this evaluation (the specific screen content tools mentioned in the previous sections are out of scope for this evaluation). It was observed that the contentaware approach achieved compression gains of 7.4% in H.264 and 6.9% in HEVC (average BD-SSIM), by simply prioritizing encoding tools with a larger impact while encoding video game content. Overall, it was observed that the ME strategy has a very significant impact on compression efficiency for video game content, while the motion refinement itself has a lower impact than for natural content. Similarly, picture partitioning and mode decision strategy have a higher weight on the compression efficiency of video game content, with the compression efficiency being somewhat less dependent on the GOP sequencing and transition management. Conclusion Motivated by the growing traffic of live video game streaming and the related esport market, we investigated, in this work, the possible encoding optimizations and normative toolset to best compress and stream game content. We first identify the main distinguished signal characteristics of game content in comparison to natural content. From this knowledge, we share some practical examples of relevant encoding strategies into an optimized HEVC encoder that provide significant improvements in compression efficiency or encode runtime/CPU cycle saving in the context of video game coding. The suggested optimization techniques are ranging from bitrate trading and AQP within a GOP, frame-adaptative deblocking and smoother in-loop reference sample filtering, the use of 10-bit encoding accuracy to adaptive motion precision estimation, and fast subpel ME. All combined, they show potential for about 10% average BD-rate gain in compression efficiency. Additionally, we review normative SCC-related tools, as adopted in HEVC SCC extension and VVC, discuss their design, and assess their compression performance for game content based on reference SW models. This specific toolset provides substantial bitrate saving for the same MS-SSIM or PSNR score with the main interesting features being the IBC and the AMVR. Finally, leveraging on AI-based content-aware method, we report that compression efficiency can be improved by 7% in H.264 or HEVC-optimized implementations by simply prioritizing encoding tools with a larger impact while encoding videogame content. 17 “Segmented” form means that the active lines from the total progressive frame, in this case 1080, are divided into odd-numbered lines (540) in a first segment, and the remaining even-numbered lines (540) in a second segment. The segment occurrence rate is then twice the progressive frame rate. There are two differences between this form and the more familiar interlaced form. First, this mode is confined to applications where the original source prior to segmentation has been scanned with a progressive scan sensor (e.g. film); this means that the motion phase of the two segments will be the same (which is not the case with true interlaced scanning). Second, it is required that there be no additional built-in vertical response filtering (e.g. by line-averaging in the sensor), as is the case with interlaced scanning, and which is present to prevent small area flicker and aliasing in interlaced displays. This is because “segmented” signals are intended to be converted back to progressive scan at some later stage. The purpose of this segmentation is to allow easier adaptation of equipment designed originally for interlaced operation, such as VTRs, and also via the doubling of effective vertical rate (in this case from 24 Hz to 48 Hz) to allow simple monitoring with a tolerable flicker frequency.

Goldman is senior vice president technology, TV compression, at Ericsson, where he is focused on video compression related products and solutions. He has been actively involved in the development of digital TV systems since 1992. Goldman was a prominent participant in the Moving Picture Experts Group, where he helped create the MPEG-2 Systems standard. He also has been influential in other industry organizations, including the SMPTE Advanced Television Systems Committee, the Digital Video Broadcasting project, and the Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers. Four of his projects have been recognized by Technology & Engineering Emmy Awards. Goldman received bachelor (high honors) and master of sciences degrees in electrical engineering from Worcester Polytechnic Institute. He holds six patents related to digital video transport. A SMPTE Fellow, he is also a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and an inductee of the Academy of Digital Television Pioneers. Goldman is currently serving as executive vice president on the SMPTE Board of Governors.

Hyper Text Mark Up Language. The Hypertext Mark-up Language (HTML) is a simple mark-up language used to create hypertext documents that are platform independent. See the World Wide Web (W3C) consortium web site at: http://www.w3.org/MarkUp/

Universal Time Co-ordinated. A method of defining time absolutely relative to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). Typically of the form: "CCYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ+n" where the "+n" defines the number of hours from GMT. See ISO DIS8601.

Elliptic Curve Cryptosystems Digital Signature Algorithm (ECCDSA). Elliptic curve cryptosystems are analogues of public-key cryptosystems such as RSA in which modular multiplication is replaced by the elliptic curve addition operation. See: V. S. Miller. Use of elliptic curves in cryptography. In Advances in Cryptology - Crypto '85, pages 417-426, Springer-Verlag, 1986.

Secure Electronic Transaction Specification, Version 1.0, May 31, 1997. Supports credit and debit card payments using certificates at the Consumer and Merchant to help ensure authenticity. Download from: < http://www.setco.org >.

Open Profiling Standard. A proposed standard which provides a framework with built-in privacy safeguards for the trusted exchange of profile information between individuals and web sites. Being developed by Netscape and Microsoft amongst others.

Secure Channel Credit Debit. A method of conducting a credit or debit card payment where unauthorised access to account information is prevented through use of secure channel transport mechanisms such as SSL/TLS. An IOTP supplement describing how SCCD works is under development.

The particular profile used for placing internationalized strings in the DNS is called "nameprep", described in Hoffman, P. and M. Blanchet, "Nameprep: A Stringprep Profile for Internationalized Domain Names", Work in Progress.

In an early stage of the process that created the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), a "Green Paper" was released by the US Government. That paper introduced new terminology and some concepts not needed by traditional DNS operations. The term "registry" was applied to the actual operator and database holder of a domain (typically at the top level, since the Green Paper was little concerned with anything else), while organizations that marketed names and made them available to "registrants" were known as "registrars". In the classic DNS model, the function of "zone administrator" encompassed both registry and registrar roles, although that model did not anticipate a commercial market in names.

The Multilingual Internet Names Consortium, http://www.minc.org/ has been an early advocate for the importance of expansion of DNS names to accommodate non-ASCII characters. Some of their specific proposals, while helping people to understand the problems better, were not compatible with the design of the DNS.
